« Je ne suis pas un cinéaste, je suis ju: “I’m not a filmmaker, I’m just a father who used a medium to defend a cause”
Gioberti François et son fils Quincy, en: Gioberti François and his son Quincy, in an interview with MP and parliamentary secretary Greg Fergus
« Je ne suis pas un cinéaste, je suis ju: “I’m not a filmmaker, I’m just a father who used a medium to defend a cause,” says Gioberti François. His work, the documentary Approuvé par le ministère de l’Éducation, was made with his son Quincy, now 15. The film recounts painful events that took place in 2018 and the steps that followed over the next two years. “We were coming back from a basketball tournament, and he was reading a book the school had recommended,” the father recalls. His son’s sports commitments force him to catch up on schoolwork on the road. While his father drives, Quincy, who attends École des Cavaliers in Aylmer, reads a book aloud. He reads a sentence that contains the N-word.
« Je lui ai demandé de la relire, mais j: “I asked him to read it again, but I did it with an aggressive emotion because I was stunned,” says Gioberti, who couldn’t believe his ears. He pulled over to the side of the road. “Quincy didn’t understand why he was being scolded; he thought it was his pronunciation. I had to reassure him,” says Mr. François, who now regrets his sharp reaction. “Imagine, my son was in Grade 6. It’s an elementary school book that has been approved by the Ministry of Education for 22 years,” he says, adding that the N-word appears three times in the book, titled Un cadavre de classe and published in 1997 by Quebec author Robert Soulières. With his son, Gioberti François was starting out on a journey whose outcome he could never have imagined.
Gioberti François, et son fils Quincy Ph: Gioberti François and his son Quincy. Photo: Courtesy
Élève studieux, Quincy ne fera pas son d: A studious pupil, Quincy would not do his homework that time. Mr. François contacted his son’s school in Gatineau. “I wrote a letter to the school to express my anger, but also my openness about the situation, if they were willing to take certain steps,” he says. The principal never called him back. “I had to contact the school board,” says Mr. François. At the Commission scolaire des Portages-de-l’Outaouais (CSPO), he was told the book was the chosen way to open up a discussion about racism.
Il décide donc de porter sa cause devant: He then decided to take his case to the Ministry of Education, where he was told the matter was up to the school. Yet it is the Ministry that authorizes the readings on school curricula. At one point, he learned that the book in question had been withdrawn. He suspects this was a response to media pressure. The book can nevertheless still be read by students across Quebec. Mr. François, who went through all of his own schooling in Quebec, from elementary school to university, can’t get over it. “I couldn’t believe that the system that had educated me could offer such a book to my son, and on top of that fight to keep it! It was something that had to be denounced.” The father then turned to the Quebec Human Rights and Youth Rights Commission, then to the Quebec Ombudsman, to no avail.
À la suite des réponses obtenues des dif: After the answers he received from the various bodies, Mr. François decided to make a documentary, which would be titled Approuvé par le ministère de l’Éducation. For this marketing specialist and avid film lover, there was everything to learn about the craft of filmmaking. Why make a film, then? “It was a complex situation; there were several stages. I think audiovisual is the easiest way to take in something in an intelligible way,” he says. But above all, he didn’t want all of this to end on a bitter note.
« C’est une situation qui est très négat: “It’s a very negative situation. I told myself I could take that situation and turn it into something positive,” he says. He and his son would get to live something new, explore a whole new field together, then share their experience. “Maybe he’ll catch the bug for film and production, I told myself. And maybe it would be more than a negative experience, because it’s a very sensitive and hard subject. For my son too, it was something very difficult to explain. I told myself that, through this experience – producing a documentary – we would not only learn things together, but also spend time together and do something positive for the community.” His family pitched in throughout the process.
« Il y a des scènes qui ne sont pas parf: “There are scenes that aren’t perfect and that my children filmed – I think it was authentic.” Completing the film was a major undertaking that required two years of work, in the middle of the pandemic, and the help of professionals. “Producing a documentary is a real profession that requires expertise in sound and image,” he points out. Approuvé par le ministère de l’Éducation was shown at the Ottawa Black Film Festival and at the 38th edition of the Vues d’Afrique film festival. Mr. François also had the opportunity to present it to students in the province.
La production du documentaire a mené la: Making the documentary took the François family from Toronto to Halifax. “What was important was to bring together the people involved and interview them based on their experience and their responsibility,” explains Mr. François. Quincy thus had the chance to interview Greg Fergus, the MP for their riding, parliamentary secretary and former chair of the Black Caucus in Ottawa. The team also met Willie O’Ree, the first Black player in the National Hockey League, historian Frantz Voltaire and professor Rachel Zellars. Mr. François also spoke with Raymond Sunstrum, a father who took the same steps he did 25 years earlier, an experience he recounts in the book La poésie de la vérité. His daughter had been exposed to an exercise containing the N-word. “They bore the brunt of the education system’s wrath, the school’s in particular,” says Mr. François, at a time when the current premier, François Legault, was education minister.
Suivant son idée initiale, M. François a: Although he started with an initial idea, Mr. François discovered the film’s storyline as the project went along. “I had a guiding thread when I thought about the documentary, but on the ground, it took on an unexpected dimension. For that reason, I believe the result is authentic, and I’m very proud of it!” exclaims the father. Every conversation led him to rethink his own position and, at times, to question himself and redirect his research. “My goal was more to expose the situation,” says the budding producer. The other thing he wanted to show, not only to his son but to all children, is the determination needed in certain situations. “When you’re exposed to a situation that hurts you, find ways to defend yourself,” advises Mr. François. He reiterates that he is neither an activist nor a filmmaker, but only a father. “A father who was hurt by a situation and who felt the need to fight against the system, but also to show his son that it’s important to fight for your convictions,” he adds. For him, it is the duty of any parent. “And that’s what motivated me and kept the flame alive during the two years of production.”

S’il pouvait changer une chose à cette h: If he could change one thing about this story, Gioberti François says it would be his reaction when his son was reading aloud. “I was very emotional in the moment. I startled him, I yelled; he wondered if he had done something wrong. I’ll blame myself for the rest of my life!” he says.
Ensuite, M. François a pris le temps d’e: Afterward, Mr. François took the time to explain to Quincy what he had just read. “He was very shocked, angry,” he says. It’s a heavy burden for a child to carry. When his teacher asked him for his homework, the boy answered: “My dad said it wasn’t an appropriate book for me.” The father, who does not wish to take part in the debate over the use, or the definition, of the N-word, reflects: “I think that word has to be handled responsibly in the curriculum if they insist on including it, especially if they’re speaking to elementary school students,” he says. The Ottawa-Carleton District School Board (OCDSB), a school board with 143 schools, 113 of them elementary, has abolished the use of that word in its curriculum. The father believes this is a step forward. “It’s something we should think about, especially when we’re talking about elementary school children. Of course, at university, it can be debated. That’s really where the confusion lies,” he says.
Si le documentaire est destiné à un publ: While the documentary is intended for audiences of all ages, the producer now realizes that some of the students it was shown to were too young. “Although I think we’re bringing something that will raise their awareness and sensitize them, I also believe children aren’t ready for this content. I think there’s an age for everything, and children need time to gain emotional and intellectual maturity before dealing with this word, which carries a great deal of historical weight,” he says. Four years after the start of this adventure, Gioberti François has lost faith in the system. “I think it’s important that schools understand diversity, since we entrust our children to them every day. We place a lot of trust in them, and it’s important that they honour that trust.
Exposer nos enfants à du contenu qui pou: Exposing our children to content that could affect their self-esteem is something dangerous that they have to take into account,” he says. Today, he keeps a close eye on the content his children are exposed to. He believes that in a situation like this, many people would have given up along the way. “I think I did this for all those parents, and I hope it will inspire parents, not to make a documentary, but to make an effort to speak out.” The impact may be felt beyond what we are able to observe. “It will help my children’s children, the children of white parents too. It helps build a more harmonious community. I think we’ll all come out ahead.” To learn more about the documentary Approuvé par le ministère de l’Éducation and Gioberti François’s journey, visit: www.filtrage.org/
